name: passkey
intent: Restrict a constructor or method to chosen collaborators by requiring a token that only those collaborators can construct, so the operation stays in the public signature while remaining uncallable by everyone else - compile-time access control instead of blanket friendship.
problem: A specific collaborator must call a constructor or method that must not become public API: a factory or helper that has to construct an object through a public constructor (make_unique, MakeGarbageCollected), a serialisation or framework layer that must reach one private hook, a subsystem that needs one internal operation, a test helper that must build a type in a state users cannot. The blunt mechanisms all miss: making the member public hands it to the world, friend (or its nearest equivalent) hands the collaborator the whole private surface, package/module/assembly access opens it to an entire scope, and a private constructor plus a factory just moves the gate into the factory. What is missing is a way to say 'this collaborator, and only this collaborator, may call exactly this operation'.
context: Statically checked code where the operation must stay visible in the type system (templates, frameworks and helper functions must be able to resolve the call) but must not be callable without a value that only the designated collaborators can create. The grant is a source-level construct checked by the compiler: the token is empty, disappears at run time and is never a defence against an adversary. Typical settings are factory-created types, library internals exposed to one subsystem, framework hooks, constructor or overload disambiguation, and test seams.
benefits: Granular instead of all-or-nothing: only the operations that take the token are reachable, while friendship (or the language's nearest equivalent) would hand the collaborator the entire private surface - the rest of the internals stay private and free to change.
The grant is declared in the signature: a reader and the compiler both see that the operation requires a key, and a caller that cannot produce one is rejected before the program runs.

Delegation becomes an explicit, first-class decision: an authorised collaborator can hand a key to a function or object it chooses (and a non-copyable key can forbid exactly that), so the authorisation graph is data instead of a set of friend declarations.
Effectively free at run time: the classic token is an empty object passed by value - a few bytes of argument space that optimisers erase - with no registration, lookup or check.

Composes and disambiguates: one key per collaborator or per group (multi-type keys authorise from any subset), and the token doubles as a tag that selects an otherwise ambiguous constructor or overload without inventing a fake parameter.
Keeps internals out of the build system: tests and tools no longer need '#define private public'-style hacks or friend-everything test builds, because the key is the documented seam.
tradeoffs: Compile-time only and defeatable: preprocessor tricks, reflection, a debugger or a patched binary step over it, so it must never be sold as a security boundary against untrusted code - only as encapsulation against accident.

Signature pollution and ceremony: every restricted operation carries a parameter that means nothing at run time, and the key type becomes part of the API surface that has to be exported, versioned and moved together with the pair of types.

Keys leak: the classic token is copyable, so a collaborator that stores one (a cache, a registry, a long-lived object) silently extends the grant; a non-copyable key closes that hole but also forbids deliberate delegation - the choice is a real design decision.

Construction holes are easy to open by accident: on pre-C++20 toolchains an empty key with a defaulted but private constructor can still be aggregate-initialised, and a key whose copy constructor is public can be minted from a null-pointer dereference (Mertz).
The grant is fixed at compile time and couples two types: changing who may call an operation is a source change on both sides, and access cannot be granted per user, per request or at run time.
Debugging is source-only: the token has no runtime identity, so an unexpected call cannot be traced through the value - the answer lives with whoever was able to construct the key.

participants.responsibility: Owns the operation - a constructor or method - and requires a key parameter for it; it declares no friends and widens no public contract, which is precisely why the key exists.

Empty value type whose construction is restricted to the authorised collaborator (a private constructor plus friendship in C++, a restricted scope elsewhere); it carries no data and no behaviour and travels by normal value semantics.
The factory, framework layer, subsystem or test helper the key was created for: it constructs keys (or receives one from its own authoriser) and calls the restricted operation.
A further function or object that receives a key from the authorised collaborator and can therefore call the same operation - intended when the key is copyable, forbidden when it is non-copyable.

use_cases: Factory-created objects with a public constructor: base::PassKey in Chromium exists for classes that a helper template (blink::MakeGarbageCollected) must construct while user code must not.
Serialisation and framework hooks: an archive, visitor or framework calls exactly one hook of a user type; the key names the framework instead of befriending it and exposing everything else.

Library-internal operations: one subsystem (allocator, persistence layer, test infrastructure) needs to construct or mutate a type users must not reach - the key names the subsystem where the language allows it, and module or assembly scope carries the rest.
Tests: a test helper constructs an otherwise unreachable state without '#define private public' builds, friend-everything test seams or reflection.
Constructor and overload disambiguation: a tag only the factory can produce selects the trusted overload and keeps the same argument list from being callable by everyone.
Deliberate delegation and revocation: the collaborator passes a key to another function that then performs the call, and a non-copyable key stops the ability from travelling further.
KDE Frameworks' KColorScheme (Frameworks 6.6.0) adopted a passkey specifically to avoid private-constructor issues, showing the idiom in a public Qt-based framework API.
Chromium's Mojo ProtoWrapperBytes uses base::PassKey to let named network, component and test classes access wrapped protobuf bytes while ordinary callers cannot supply the operation.
Abseil's C++ Tip of the Week #134 uses a passkey token with std::make_shared so a factory can keep single-allocation construction without making unconstrained construction the public API.
avoid_when: The collaborator needs the whole private surface: a single friend declaration (or the language's nearest equivalent) says it with less code; the token pays off only when the grant is a strict subset.

The language already names the grant: Rust's pub(in path), Scala's private[C], Swift's fileprivate and the package/module scopes of Java, C# and Kotlin express module- or package-shaped grants directly - do not hand-build a token for them.
The operation is a legitimate part of the contract: make it public or extract an interface instead of hiding it behind a key every reader has to look up.
The goal is to stop untrusted callers: use runtime enforcement (a reference monitor, capability objects with real checks, complete mediation), because the compiler erases the token.
The language cannot enforce it and the token would be a convention (C, Python, Ruby): the code would say more than the compiler does, and a real boundary elsewhere is the honest alternative.
anti_patterns: Publicly constructible key: the key's constructor (or the key type itself) is exported to the world, so anyone can 'be authorised' and the token decorates signatures without protecting anything.
Security theatre: presenting the passkey as protection against malicious code while macros, reflection, a debugger or a patched binary reach the same member.
Key with state or logic: putting bookkeeping, validation or decisions inside the token, which turns an empty marker into a component that can fail, be reused or be forged with better arguments.
Leaky grant: the authorised collaborator stores keys in a cache, registry or global 'for convenience', so every later caller becomes authorised without anyone deciding to authorise it.
Key everywhere: tokenising every internal operation until the signatures are noise - friendship with worse ergonomics and no reduction in coupling.
Bypass builds: keeping '#define private public' or a reflection-based test seam next to the key, so the discipline the key encodes is quietly optional.
design_principles: Least authority: hand out the smallest callable surface that lets the collaborator do its job - one operation, not the private surface.
Explicitness: the grant is declared in a signature and in a type, not implied by ambient scope, naming conventions or a documentation comment.
Correctness by construction: an unauthorised call is a compile error where the language can express it, not a check that may or may not run later.
Encapsulation and information hiding: the implementation stays private and the public contract stays stable while the collaborator's access is carved out beside it.
Interface segregation: the collaborator depends on the operation it may call, not on the class internals that a friendship would expose.
Delegation as a design decision: whether the ability may be passed on (copyable key) or must stay with the named collaborator (non-copyable key) is stated in the token's type, not left to chance.
best_practices: Keep the token empty, unnamed and passed by value: no state, no behaviour, no name at the call site - it documents the requirement and nothing else.

Restrict every way of building one: private (or scope-restricted) default and copy constructors. On pre-C++20 toolchains make the default constructor user-provided, because aggregate initialisation ignores a defaulted private one, and keep the copy constructor private so a null-pointer dereference cannot mint a key.

Make the construction scope as small as the language allows - a nested type, a type nested in the authorised collaborator, or module/file/assembly scope - and write down which one it is next to the declaration.
Choose the copy policy deliberately: copyable when the collaborator is expected to delegate, non-copyable (deleted copy and move) when the grant must stay put.

Never widen the grant silently: do not export the key type or its constructor from a broader scope, do not store keys in long-lived shared state, and do not let helpers hand out keys they were not authorised to hand out.
Say in the code that the boundary is compile-time encapsulation against accident, and keep runtime mediation (checks, capabilities, reference monitors) for callers you do not trust.
sources: Chromium, 'The Passkey Pattern' (chromium/src docs/patterns/passkey.md) - the catalog's citation: expose a subset of a class's methods by requiring a token only specific classes can construct; the token is 'effectively free at runtime' and may be delegated by passing it on.

Arne Mertz, 'Passkey Idiom: More Useful Empty Classes', Simplify C++ (19 October 2016); reprinted as 'Passkey Idiom: A Useful Empty Class', ACCU Overload 31(176), August 2023 - friendship is all-or-nothing, the ConstructorKey shape, and the aggregate-initialisation and null-pointer copy-constructor holes.
KDE, Frameworks 6.6.0 release notes - KColorScheme uses a passkey to avoid issues with a private constructor, a concrete framework use of a token-gated construction seam.
Chromium Mojo, proto_wrapper_passkeys.h - mojo::base::ProtoWrapperBytes exposes direct protobuf byte access only to named friend classes through base::PassKey.
Abseil Tip of the Week #134 - recommends the passkey idiom for retaining single-allocation std::make_shared while guarding a constructor, and documents the pre-C++20 aggregate-initialisation caveat.

Xaizek, 'C++11+ aggregate initializer surprise' - criticism of deleted/defaulted empty passkey constructors: aggregate initialization can bypass intended access checks unless the constructor is user-provided.
